title: Keywords, identifiers, constants, and variables
sourceLabel: C Preliminaries: Keywords, Identifiers, Constants, and Variables.
objectives: Explain that a keyword is a word C already owns.
Write legal identifiers and reject illegal ones.
Tell a constant from a variable.
Describe a variable as a named box in memory that holds a value of a type.
completionCriteria: Classify ten tokens as keyword, identifier, or illegal.
Give one named constant and one variable in a one-line story.

notes.introduction: C programs are built from words and names. Some words are reserved. Some names we invent. Some values never change. Some boxes in memory can change.
notes.beginner: A keyword is a word the C language already uses, such as int or return. You must not reuse it as a name. An identifier is a name you invent for a variable, a function, or similar — letters, digits, and underscore, not starting with a digit. A constant is a value that does not change, such as 10 or 'A'. A variable is a named place in memory whose value can change while the program runs.
notes.formal: A keyword is a reserved identifier specified by the C standard that has a fixed meaning. An identifier is a sequence of letters, digits, and underscores beginning with a letter or underscore. A constant is a literal or an object whose value is not updated. A variable is an object with a name, a type, and storage, whose stored value may be replaced.

terms.meaning: A reserved word (int, return, if, while, …). You cannot use it as your variable name.
A name you choose that follows C's spelling rules.
A value written directly, such as 25, 3.14, 'C', or "hi".
A named memory location with a type. Its contents can change.
Telling C the name and type of a variable, for example int rolls;
Putting a value into a variable with = .

revision: Keywords are reserved. int marks is illegal as a second meaning of int.
Identifiers: start with letter or _; then letters, digits, _.
Constant stays; variable can be overwritten.
notes.examAnswer: Keywords are reserved words with fixed meaning in C. Identifiers are user-defined names that must start with a letter or underscore. A constant is a fixed value. A variable is a named typed object in memory whose value may change.

body.objectives: After this lesson you can look at a short line of C and say which words the language owns and which words you invented.
body.prerequisiteCheck: You can follow numbered steps (topic 2). You know a computer has memory (topic 1). We now give pieces of memory names.
body.introduction: English has words that are already taken ('the', 'and'). C does too. If you name a variable int, the compiler becomes confused because int already means 'integer type'.
body.analogy: A classroom has reserved seats labelled 'Teacher'. Students may not sit there. Those seats are keywords. Students write their own names on other seats — identifiers. A painted room number that never changes is a constant. A chalkboard that you wipe and rewrite is a variable.
body.explanation:
C is case-sensitive. Score and score are different identifiers. Keywords in standard C are lowercase: int, char, float, double, return, if, else, while, for, void, and others. You do not need to recode the entire keyword list tonight; you need the rule: if the word is in the language, it is not yours.

Identifier rules used in first-year teaching: start with a letter or underscore; continue with letters, digits, or underscore; no spaces; no special signs like @ or -. roll_no is legal. 1roll is not (starts with a digit). roll-no is not (minus sign). Prefer clear names: marks, not m.

A constant is a value you write in the program. 42 is an integer constant. 3.5 is a floating constant. 'A' is a character constant (single quotes). "A" is a string literal (double quotes) — that difference matters later. const int MAX = 50; is a named constant in modern teaching; older notes also use #define MAX 50. Both mean 'do not treat this like a changing box'.

A variable is declared with a type and a name: int marks; That asks memory for a box that can hold an int. marks = 18; stores 18. marks = 20; replaces it. The name stays; the contents change. Until you assign, the box may hold leftover garbage — so beginners should initialise: int marks = 0;

examples.title: Legal and illegal identifiers
steps: int — illegal as a name, it is a keyword.
Choose roll_no for a student roll in this academy (format rules of the college are still unresolved; this is only a C name).

examples.title: Variable versus constant
steps: int cups = 2;  cups is a variable. cups = cups + 1; is allowed.
Writing 1 = cups; is meaningless. You cannot assign to a literal.

body.execution: Trace int n = 4; n = n + 2; Memory starts with n holding 4. The right-hand side reads 4, adds 2, gets 6. Then 6 is written into n. After the statement, n is 6. The identifier n never changed; the stored value did.

trace.prompt: After int a = 5; a = 8; what value is in a?

predict.prompt: Is 2total a legal identifier? Answer yes or no.

mistakes: Using a keyword as a variable name (int, return, void).
Thinking Score and score are the same. C is case-sensitive.
Forgetting to initialise. Uninitialised locals can hold anything.

guided.prompt: Which of these are keywords: int, marks, return, total? List the keywords only.

independent.prompt: Invent a legal identifier for 'number of present students' and write one declaration that starts it at 0.

check.prompt: A variable is best described as:
choices: A named memory location whose value can change

check.prompt: Write the character constant for capital B (include quotes in the C sense: single quotes).

body.summary: Keywords are reserved. Identifiers are your names, spelled with letters, digits, and _. Constants stay put. Variables are named typed boxes in memory that you may overwrite. Initialise them.
